AL.note: Alabama is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
AL.police_in_public: The Eleventh Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police conduct in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)).

AK.note: Alaska is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
AK.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)).

AZ.note: Arizona is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
AZ.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)). Arizona's 2022 law banning filming of police from within 8 feet (A.R.S. § 13-3732, HB 2319) was permanently blocked by a federal court in July 2023 (Arizona Broadcasters Ass'n v. Mayes, D. Ariz.) and cannot be enforced.

AR.note: Arkansas is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
AR.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

CA.note: California requires all parties' consent to record a confidential conversation, and all parties' consent to record any call involving a cell or cordless phone. Conversations in public where people could reasonably expect to be overheard are not 'confidential'.
CA.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)). California law also states that photographing or recording an officer in a public place, or from a place you have a right to be, is not by itself obstruction (Cal. Penal Code § 148(g)).

CO.note: Colorado is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
CO.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)). Colorado law also gives you a statutory right to record any incident involving a peace officer if you do not interfere, and limits seizure of your recording (C.R.S. §§ 16-3-311, 13-21-128).

CT.citation: Conn. Gen. Stat. §§ 53a-187, 53a-189 (criminal: one-party); § 52-570d (civil: all-party for phone calls)
CT.note: Connecticut lets you record an in-person conversation you are part of, but recording a phone call without everyone's consent (or a recorded warning) can make you liable in a civil suit.
CT.police_in_public: The Second Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so the state consent law does not apply to them.
CT.issue: App labels Connecticut all-party for all recordings; the all-party rule (§ 52-570d) applies only to phone calls and only for civil liability, and in-person recording is one-party.

DE.citation: 11 Del. C. § 1335(a)(4) (privacy law: all-party); 11 Del. C. § 2402(c)(4) (wiretap law: one-party)
DE.note: Delaware's two laws conflict: the wiretap law allows one-party consent, but the privacy law bars intercepting private conversations without all parties' consent, so follow the stricter all-party rule for private conversations.
DE.police_in_public: The Third Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police doing their official duties in public (Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017)).
DE.issue: App omits Delaware and defaults it to one-party; RCFP lists Delaware among all-party states because of the conflicting privacy statute.

DC.note: D.C. is a one-party consent jurisdiction: you may record a conversation or call you are part of without telling the others.
DC.police_in_public: The D.C. Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so D.C.'s one-party law does not bar recording them.

FL.note: Florida requires all parties' consent to record a private conversation or call, but the law protects only conversations where the speaker had a reasonable expectation of privacy.
FL.police_in_public: The Eleventh Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police conduct in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)). Since January 1, 2025, Florida also makes it a misdemeanor to stay within 25 feet of a first responder after a verbal warning if you intend to impede, threaten or harass them (Fla. Stat. § 843.31).
FL.issue: App note says recording police in public is 'generally protected' without naming the 11th Circuit authority or the 2025 25-foot buffer law.

GA.note: Georgia is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
GA.police_in_public: The Eleventh Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police conduct in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000)).

HI.note: Hawaii lets you record a conversation you are part of, but installing or using a recording device in a private place (like a home) to capture sounds not audible outside requires consent of the people entitled to privacy there.
HI.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)). The Hawaii Supreme Court also protects filming officials performing duties in public under the First Amendment and the Hawaii Constitution (State v. Russo, 141 Haw. 181 (2017)), and § 711-1111 does not apply to officers who have no reasonable expectation of privacy.
HI.issue: App treats Hawaii as plain one-party; RCFP classes it as mixed because of the private-place rule.

ID.note: Idaho is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
ID.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)).

IL.citation: 720 ILCS 5/14-2(a), as amended by Pub. Act 98-1142 (eff. Dec. 30, 2014); 720 ILCS 5/14-1
IL.note: Illinois makes it a crime to secretly record a private conversation without all parties' consent; recording conversations where no one reasonably expects privacy is not covered.
IL.police_in_public: Recording police performing duties in public is legal: the Seventh Circuit held the old law could not be applied to it (ACLU of Illinois v. Alvarez, 679 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2012)), the Illinois Supreme Court struck the old law down (People v. Melongo, 2014 IL 114852; People v. Clark, 2014 IL 115776), and the 2014 rewrite covers only surreptitious recording of private conversations.
IL.issue: App note cites a nonexistent case 'People v. ACLU of Ill.'; the controlling authorities are ACLU of Illinois v. Alvarez (7th Cir. 2012), People v. Melongo and People v. Clark (Ill. 2014), and the Dec. 2014 amendment.

IN.citation: Ind. Code § 35-33.5-5-5 (phone/electronic); in-person recording not addressed by statute
IN.note: Indiana requires at least one party's consent to record a phone or electronic communication; no statute addresses recording in-person conversations.
IN.police_in_public: The Seventh Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to audio-record police performing their duties in public (ACLU of Illinois v. Alvarez, 679 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2012)). Indiana's 25-foot police buffer law (Ind. Code § 35-44.1-2-14, 2023, amended 2025) is blocked: the Seventh Circuit affirmed a preliminary injunction on vagueness grounds on Aug. 5, 2025 (No. 24-2927) and remanded on the injunction's scope, though an earlier panel had rejected a separate First Amendment challenge (Nicodemus v. City of South Bend).

IA.note: Iowa is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
IA.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

KS.citation: Kan. Stat. Ann. § 21-6101; State v. Roudybush, 235 Kan. 834 (1984)
KS.note: Kansas is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
KS.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)).

KY.note: Kentucky is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
KY.police_in_public: The Sixth Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so open recording from a place you are allowed to be is not covered by the consent law.

LA.note: Louisiana is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
LA.police_in_public: The Fifth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017)). Louisiana's 2024 law making it a crime to approach within 25 feet of an officer after being told to stay back (Act 291, HB 173, La. R.S. 14:109) was preliminarily blocked by a federal court on Jan. 31, 2025 (Deep South Today v. Murrill, M.D. La.); the state appealed to the Fifth Circuit.

ME.citation: Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 15, §§ 709, 710 (one-party); tit. 17-A, § 511 (private places)
ME.note: Maine lets you record a conversation you are part of, but recording in a private place (such as a bathroom or changing room) sounds not audible outside requires consent of everyone entitled to privacy there.
ME.police_in_public: The First Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to openly record police doing their jobs in public (Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Gericke v. Begin, 753 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2014)), unless the recording interferes with their duties.
ME.issue: App treats Maine as plain one-party; RCFP classes it as mixed because of the private-place rule.

MD.citation: Md. Code Ann., Cts. & Jud. Proc. §§ 10-401, 10-402
MD.note: Maryland requires all parties' consent to record a private in-person conversation and any phone call; in-person conversations with no reasonable expectation of privacy are not covered.
MD.police_in_public: Police doing their jobs in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, and the Fourth Circuit has treated recording or livestreaming a police traffic stop as First Amendment activity (Sharpe v. Town of Winterville, 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023)); officers may still impose reasonable safety limits.
MD.issue: App note omits that the consent rule applies only to private in-person conversations and says nothing about recording police.

MA.note: Massachusetts bans secretly recording any conversation without all parties' consent; open recording that everyone can see is not 'secret' and is not covered.
MA.police_in_public: The First Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to openly record police doing their jobs in public (Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Gericke v. Begin, 753 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2014)), unless the recording interferes with their duties. The First Circuit also held the law cannot be applied to secretly recording police officers performing their duties in public (Project Veritas Action Fund v. Rollins, 982 F.3d 813 (1st Cir. 2020)).

MI.citation: Mich. Comp. Laws § 750.539c; Sullivan v. Gray, 117 Mich. App. 476 (1982)
MI.note: Michigan's eavesdropping law bars recording a private conversation without all parties' consent, but courts have held a participant may record a conversation they are part of (Sullivan v. Gray); the Michigan Supreme Court has not decided the issue.
MI.police_in_public: The Sixth Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so open recording from a place you are allowed to be is not covered by the consent law.
MI.issue: App labels Michigan strict all-party; under Sullivan v. Gray the all-party rule applies to non-participants and a participant may record, and the question is unsettled.

MN.note: Minnesota is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
MN.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

MS.note: Mississippi is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
MS.police_in_public: The Fifth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017)).

MO.note: Missouri lets you record a phone call you are part of; the in-person rule is unclear because few cases interpret it, so RCFP advises getting everyone's consent before recording a private in-person conversation.
MO.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.
MO.issue: App treats Missouri as plain one-party; RCFP classes in-person recording as all-party and the statute is unclear.

MT.note: Montana makes it a crime to record a conversation without the knowledge of all parties; in-person, the ban targets hidden devices, and if one party warns that the conversation is being recorded either side may record.
MT.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)).
MT.issue: App note omits that open (non-hidden) recording and recording in public places are not covered.

NE.note: Nebraska is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
NE.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

NV.citation: Nev. Rev. Stat. § 200.620 (phone: all-party); § 200.650 (in-person: one-party); Lane v. Allstate Ins. Co., 114 Nev. 1176 (1998)
NV.note: Nevada lets you record an in-person conversation you are part of, but recording a phone call requires all parties' consent (Lane v. Allstate), and the Nevada Supreme Court applies that rule to cell calls and texts.
NV.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)).
NV.issue: App defaults Nevada to one-party; phone recording requires all-party consent under NRS 200.620 and Lane v. Allstate.

NH.note: New Hampshire requires all parties' consent to record a phone call or an in-person conversation where people reasonably expect not to be recorded.
NH.police_in_public: The First Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to openly record police doing their jobs in public (Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Gericke v. Begin, 753 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2014)), unless the recording interferes with their duties.

NJ.note: New Jersey is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
NJ.police_in_public: The Third Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police doing their official duties in public (Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017)).

NM.note: New Mexico requires one party's consent to record a landline call; its statute does not cover in-person conversations, and its reach to cell calls is unclear.
NM.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)).

NY.note: New York is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
NY.police_in_public: The Second Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so the state consent law does not apply to them. New York law also protects the right to record police activity if you are not under arrest or in custody and do not physically interfere, and lets you sue an officer who interferes (N.Y. Civ. Rights Law § 79-p).

NC.note: North Carolina is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
NC.police_in_public: Police doing their jobs in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, and the Fourth Circuit has treated recording or livestreaming a police traffic stop as First Amendment activity (Sharpe v. Town of Winterville, 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023)); officers may still impose reasonable safety limits.

ND.note: North Dakota is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
ND.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

OH.note: Ohio is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
OH.police_in_public: The Sixth Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so open recording from a place you are allowed to be is not covered by the consent law.

OK.note: Oklahoma is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
OK.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)).

OR.citation: Or. Rev. Stat. § 165.540(1)(a) (phone: one-party); § 165.540(1)(c) (in-person: all must be specifically informed); § 165.540(5)(b) (police exception)
OR.note: Oregon lets you record a phone call you are part of, but you must tell everyone before recording an in-person conversation; the Ninth Circuit en banc upheld that rule in 2025 (Project Veritas v. Schmidt, cert. denied Oct. 6, 2025).
OR.police_in_public: Oregon law expressly allows you to record a conversation with an on-duty officer if you record openly and in plain view, the conversation is audible to you, and you are somewhere you lawfully may be (ORS 165.540(5)(b)); the Ninth Circuit also recognizes a First Amendment right to record police in public (Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)).
OR.issue: App labels Oregon all-party for everything; phone calls are one-party and only in-person conversations require informing all parties, and the 'public officials' exception is specifically for openly recording on-duty police.

PA.note: Pennsylvania requires all parties' consent to record a phone call, and to record an in-person conversation where the speakers reasonably expect not to be overheard or recorded.
PA.police_in_public: The Third Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police doing their official duties in public (Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017)).

RI.note: Rhode Island is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
RI.police_in_public: The First Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to openly record police doing their jobs in public (Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Gericke v. Begin, 753 F.3d 1 (1st Cir. 2014)), unless the recording interferes with their duties.

SC.note: South Carolina is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
SC.police_in_public: Police doing their jobs in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, and the Fourth Circuit has treated recording or livestreaming a police traffic stop as First Amendment activity (Sharpe v. Town of Winterville, 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023)); officers may still impose reasonable safety limits.

SD.note: South Dakota is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
SD.police_in_public: The Eighth Circuit has not squarely ruled on a right to record police, though it has recognized a clearly established right to watch police in public from a non-interfering distance (Chestnut v. Wallace, 947 F.3d 1085 (8th Cir. 2020)); officers in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say.

TN.note: Tennessee is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
TN.police_in_public: The Sixth Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so open recording from a place you are allowed to be is not covered by the consent law. A 2025 Tennessee law (SB 30/HB 55, eff. July 1, 2025) makes it an offense to approach within 25 feet of an officer after being told to stop; a federal lawsuit challenging it was filed July 22, 2025 and its outcome was not confirmed.

TX.citation: Tex. Penal Code § 16.02; Tex. Code Crim. Proc. art. 18A.001
TX.note: Texas is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
TX.police_in_public: The Fifth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film and audio-record police in public, subject to reasonable time, place and manner limits (Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017)).

UT.note: Utah is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
UT.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)).

VT.citation: No Vermont recording statute; federal law applies (18 U.S.C. § 2511(2)(d))
VT.note: Vermont has no state recording law, so federal one-party consent applies: you may record a conversation you are part of unless you do it to commit a crime or tort.
VT.police_in_public: The Second Circuit has not directly ruled on a First Amendment right to record police, but officers performing duties in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, so the state consent law does not apply to them.

VA.note: Virginia is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
VA.police_in_public: Police doing their jobs in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, and the Fourth Circuit has treated recording or livestreaming a police traffic stop as First Amendment activity (Sharpe v. Town of Winterville, 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023)); officers may still impose reasonable safety limits.

WA.note: Washington requires all parties' consent to record a private conversation or call; consent is shown by an announcement that is itself recorded, and conversations in public or in front of third parties are generally not private.
WA.police_in_public: The Ninth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to record police performing official duties in public places (Fordyce v. City of Seattle, 55 F.3d 436 (9th Cir. 1995); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018)). Washington courts have held that officers' statements while making an arrest on a public street are not a private conversation (State v. Flora, 68 Wn. App. 802 (1992)).

WV.note: West Virginia is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
WV.police_in_public: Police doing their jobs in public have no expectation of privacy in what they say, and the Fourth Circuit has treated recording or livestreaming a police traffic stop as First Amendment activity (Sharpe v. Town of Winterville, 59 F.4th 674 (4th Cir. 2023)); officers may still impose reasonable safety limits.

WI.note: Wisconsin is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
WI.police_in_public: The Seventh Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to audio-record police performing their duties in public (ACLU of Illinois v. Alvarez, 679 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2012)).
WI.issue: App lists Wisconsin as all-party; Wis. Stat. § 968.31(2)(c) allows a party to the conversation to record (one-party).

WY.note: Wyoming is a one-party consent state: you may record a conversation you are part of without telling the others.
WY.police_in_public: The Tenth Circuit recognizes a First Amendment right to film police performing their duties in public (Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022)).

tips.original: You have the right to remain silent. Use it. Anything you say CAN be used against you.
tips.rewrite: You have the right to remain silent: say out loud "I am using my right to remain silent," because anything you say can be used against you.
tips.authority: U.S. Const. amend. V; Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966); Berghuis v. Thompkins, 560 U.S. 370 (2010) and Salinas v. Texas, 570 U.S. 178 (2013) (silence must be invoked clearly)
tips.issue: Accurate, but courts require you to invoke the right clearly (Berghuis, Salinas); the rewrite adds how. Several states also require you to give your name when lawfully stopped (Hiibel v. Sixth Judicial Dist., 542 U.S. 177 (2004)).

tips.original: You can legally record police in public in all 50 states as long as you don't interfere.
tips.rewrite: Federal appeals courts covering most states recognize a right to openly record police doing their jobs in public, but officers can set reasonable distance limits and some states restrict secret audio recording.
tips.authority: Glik v. Cunniffe, 655 F.3d 78 (1st Cir. 2011); Fields v. City of Philadelphia, 862 F.3d 353 (3d Cir. 2017); Turner v. Driver, 848 F.3d 678 (5th Cir. 2017); ACLU of Ill. v. Alvarez, 679 F.3d 583 (7th Cir. 2012); Askins v. DHS, 899 F.3d 1035 (9th Cir. 2018); Irizarry v. Yehia, 38 F.4th 1282 (10th Cir. 2022); Smith v. City of Cumming, 212 F.3d 1332 (11th Cir. 2000); Fla. Stat. § 843.31
tips.issue: The Second, Sixth, Eighth and D.C. Circuits have not squarely recognized the right, the right is subject to reasonable time/place/manner limits, and 25-foot buffer laws exist (Florida in force; Indiana, Louisiana and Arizona's 8-foot law blocked; Tennessee challenged).

tips.original: A DUI checkpoint must be publicly announced in advance in most US states.
tips.rewrite: Sobriety checkpoints are allowed under the U.S. Constitution, but about a dozen states do not use them, and advance-notice rules differ from state to state.
tips.authority: Michigan Dept. of State Police v. Sitz, 496 U.S. 444 (1990) (no advance-publicity requirement); checkpoints not conducted in AK, ID, IA, MI, MN, MT, OR, RI, TX, WA, WI, WY (per GHSA list; Michigan barred by Sitz v. Dept. of State Police, 443 Mich. 744 (1993) on state-constitution grounds)
tips.issue: No federal or majority-state rule requires advance announcement; publicity is a factor some state courts weigh, not a nationwide requirement. Source pages could not be fetched in this session (search budget exhausted); the state list is from GHSA and should be re-checked.

tips.original: You have 30 days to request a court date after most traffic citations.
tips.rewrite: Your traffic ticket shows the deadline to pay or contest it, and that deadline varies by state and court, so act before the date printed on the ticket.
tips.authority: State traffic codes and local court rules (no uniform national deadline)
tips.issue: There is no nationwide 30-day rule; deadlines are set by each state and court and printed on the citation.

tips.original: Police need a warrant to search your home. You can say 'I do not consent to a search.'
tips.rewrite: Police usually need a warrant to enter or search your home unless you consent or an emergency exception applies, so you can calmly say "I do not consent to a search."
tips.authority: U.S. Const. amend. IV; Payton v. New York, 445 U.S. 573 (1980); Schneckloth v. Bustamonte, 412 U.S. 218 (1973) (consent); Brigham City v. Stuart, 547 U.S. 398 (2006) and Kentucky v. King, 563 U.S. 452 (2011) (exigent circumstances); Samson v. California, 547 U.S. 843 (2006) (parolee searches)
tips.issue: Stated as absolute; warrantless home entry is allowed with consent, exigent circumstances (emergency, hot pursuit, preventing destruction of evidence), and for many people on probation or parole.

tips.original: After arrest, you have the right to one phone call. Use it to contact a lawyer.
tips.rewrite: There is no nationwide constitutional right to a phone call after arrest, though some states give one by law, so ask for a lawyer and do not discuss your case on jail phones, which are recorded.
tips.authority: No federal constitutional right; state statutes vary (e.g., Cal. Penal Code § 851.5 gives at least three calls)
tips.issue: 'One phone call' is not a constitutional right; it depends on state law and jail policy.

tips.original: An expungement can seal your arrest record — even if you were never convicted.
tips.rewrite: In most states you can ask to seal or expunge an arrest that did not lead to a conviction, though eligibility and waiting periods depend on your state.
tips.authority: State expungement/sealing statutes; Collateral Consequences Resource Center, Restoration of Rights Project (50-state comparison of non-conviction records)
tips.issue: Substantially accurate as 'can'; the rewrite adds that eligibility varies by state.

tips.original: You cannot be fired for serving on a jury. Federal law protects you.
tips.rewrite: Federal law protects your job when you serve on a federal jury, and most states have their own laws protecting state jurors, so check your state's rule.
tips.authority: 28 U.S.C. § 1875 (federal jurors only); state juror-protection statutes
tips.issue: 28 U.S.C. § 1875 covers only federal jury service; state jury service is protected by state law, which varies.

tips.original: Bail can be reduced. Ask your attorney to file a motion to reduce bail at arraignment.
tips.rewrite: If bail is set, your lawyer can ask the court to lower it at a bail hearing or by motion; some states, such as Illinois, no longer use cash bail at all.
tips.authority: U.S. Const. amend. VIII; Stack v. Boyle, 342 U.S. 1 (1951) (motion to reduce bail); Illinois Pretrial Fairness Act (Pub. Act 101-652, as amended; cash bail ended Sept. 18, 2023)
tips.issue: Substantially accurate; timing ('at arraignment') varies by state, and Illinois abolished cash bail.

tips.original: Miranda rights only apply after arrest — police can ask questions before arresting you.
tips.rewrite: Police must give Miranda warnings only before questioning someone in custody, which can happen before a formal arrest, and you can choose to stay silent at any time.
tips.authority: Miranda v. Arizona, 384 U.S. 436 (1966); Berkemer v. McCarty, 468 U.S. 420 (1984) (Miranda applies once a suspect is in custody, even for misdemeanors; ordinary traffic stops are not custody); Stansbury v. California, 511 U.S. 318 (1994)
tips.issue: Miranda is triggered by custodial interrogation, not formal arrest; a person can be 'in custody' before being arrested.

tips.original: You can refuse a field sobriety test in most states. Breathalyzer refusal has separate consequences.
tips.rewrite: In most states roadside field sobriety tests are voluntary, but refusing a breath or chemical test after a DUI arrest usually triggers license suspension under implied-consent laws.
tips.authority: State implied-consent statutes; Birchfield v. North Dakota, 579 U.S. 438 (2016)
tips.issue: Substantially accurate; refusal of field tests may still be used as evidence in some states, and preliminary roadside breath tests are mandatory in some states.

tips.original: A public defender is free. You have the right to one if you cannot afford an attorney.
tips.rewrite: If you cannot afford a lawyer and you face possible jail time, you have the right to a court-appointed lawyer, though some states may charge you a fee for it later.
tips.authority: Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963); Argersinger v. Hamlin, 407 U.S. 25 (1972); Scott v. Illinois, 440 U.S. 367 (1979); Alabama v. Shelton, 535 U.S. 654 (2002); Fuller v. Oregon, 417 U.S. 40 (1974) (recoupment allowed)
tips.issue: The constitutional right applies when imprisonment (including a suspended sentence) is imposed, not to every case, and many states charge application fees or seek repayment, so 'free' is not accurate everywhere.

tips.original: Probation violation can result in jail time. Report every scheduled check-in without exception.
tips.rewrite: A probation violation can lead to jail time, so attend every scheduled check-in.
tips.authority: Gagnon v. Scarpelli, 411 U.S. 778 (1973); Morrissey v. Brewer, 408 U.S. 471 (1972); state probation statutes

tips.original: Your employer cannot ask about arrests that didn't result in conviction in many states.
tips.rewrite: Many states bar employers from asking about arrests that did not lead to a conviction.
tips.authority: e.g., Cal. Lab. Code § 432.7; 775 ILCS 5/2-103; N.Y. Exec. Law § 296(16); Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(9); EEOC Enforcement Guidance on Arrest and Conviction Records (2012)
tips.issue: Accurate as worded ('in many states'); wording tightened.

tips.original: Possession of marijuana may be a misdemeanor or felony depending on weight — know your state's law.
tips.rewrite: Marijuana laws vary widely: adult possession is legal in many states, can be a misdemeanor or felony in others depending on the amount, and remains illegal under federal law.
tips.authority: 21 U.S.C. § 844; state cannabis statutes (NCSL cannabis overview)
tips.issue: Omits that adult-use possession is legal in many states and that federal law still prohibits possession.

app_errors_summary: WI listed all-party but is one-party (Wis. Stat. § 968.31(2)(c)).
OR is mixed (phone one-party, in-person all must be informed) with an explicit police-recording exception ORS 165.540(5)(b).
NV defaulted to one-party but phone calls require all-party consent (NRS 200.620; Lane v. Allstate).
DE defaulted to one-party but conflicting § 1335 privacy law makes all-party the safe rule.
CT is all-party only for phone calls and only civilly; MI participant recording allowed under Sullivan v. Gray.
IL note cites nonexistent case 'People v. ACLU of Ill.'.

Generic one-party note asserts a right to record police everywhere; 2nd, 6th, 8th and D.C. Circuits have not squarely held so, and buffer-zone laws exist (FL in force; TN challenged; IN, LA, AZ blocked).
